Yeah, so I think it's one of the more interesting open questions right now. Mixtral is a mixture-of-experts model, and there's this intuition a lot of people have that the experts would specialize in clean, human-interpretable ways. You know, one expert does code, one does biology, one does French. But when people have actually looked at the routing, it doesn't really look like that. The specialization seems much more syntactic or token-level, and it's kind of messy.

What Trenton's team has done with dictionary learning and sparse autoencoders is give us a way to pull apart the superposition inside a layer and find features that actually mean something. So the natural question is: if you apply that to the experts, do you find that each expert has a coherent set of features? Is the routing decision reading off particular features? Or is the expert boundary basically arbitrary from the model's point of view, with features smeared across experts the same way they're smeared across neurons?

Either answer would be really informative. If the experts are interpretable at the feature level, that tells you something about how to design and maybe even control these architectures. You could imagine steering by routing. If they're not, that's also important, because it means the architectural structure we impose doesn't necessarily line up with how the model wants to carve up the problem.

It's also a nice project because it's tractable. Mixtral is open weights, it's a reasonable size, and the tooling for sparse autoencoders has gotten good enough that someone outside a big lab could make real progress. It's the kind of thing where a motivated person could produce a result that people inside the labs would genuinely want to read. That's a good place to be if you're trying to get into the field.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing that makes Mixtral interesting here is that it's one of the only genuinely capable open-weight models where you have a sparse mixture-of-experts architecture that you can actually get your hands on. And the question that I think everyone has about MoE is: what are the experts actually doing? When you look at the routing, the surface-level answer from the papers is kind of disappointing. You see things like "this expert fires on punctuation" or "this one fires on code tokens," and it doesn't look like the clean domain specialization people imagined, where one expert does biology and another does law.

But I think that's exactly the kind of thing where the dictionary learning approach from Trenton's team becomes useful. The reason the routing looks messy is that you're looking at it through the lens of tokens, which is the wrong basis. The whole point of the sparse autoencoder work is that the model's actual units of computation are features, which are superposed and don't correspond neatly to individual tokens or neurons. So if you train sparse autoencoders on the residual stream going into the router, and on the outputs of each expert, you can start asking much more precise questions. Does the router actually route on features? Are there features that are only ever processed by a particular expert? Is there redundancy, where multiple experts have learned to compute the same feature because of load balancing pressure during training?

That last one I find really compelling from an efficiency standpoint. If you could show that experts are substantially redundant at the feature level, that tells you something about how much capacity is being wasted and how you might train these things differently. Conversely, if you found that the experts carve up feature space in a really clean way, that'd be a strong argument that MoE is doing something closer to what people hoped.

The other reason it's a good project is the one that I think matters most for actually doing research: it's tractable. Mixtral is big enough that the phenomena are real and not toy, but it's small enough that a small team or even a grad student with reasonable compute can run the full pipeline on it. A lot of the most interesting interpretability questions right now are blocked on access to frontier models. This one isn't. You can just go do it. And I think there's a lot of value in people picking the questions where the gap between "interesting" and "doable this month" is small.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting question is whether the experts in a mixture-of-experts model correspond to anything we can understand. You have this architecture that explicitly routes different tokens to different sets of parameters, but that doesn’t necessarily mean one expert does mathematics and another does French. The specialization could be much less intuitive than that.

You could use the sparse autoencoder approach to try to identify the features represented within each expert, and then look at how those features relate to routing. Are particular features concentrated in particular experts? Are the same features duplicated across experts? What information is the router using to make its decision?

That gives you something concrete to investigate beyond just finding an interesting-looking feature. You can intervene on a feature or change the routing and see whether the model’s behavior changes in the way your explanation predicts. And even if the experts don’t have clean, human-readable roles, understanding why they don’t would tell us something useful about how these models organize computation.

sol-6.1.text:
Because Mixtral gives you an interesting test of what the experts are actually doing. You have this mixture-of-experts architecture, where different tokens get routed to different parts of the network, but that doesn’t necessarily mean each expert has some clean, human-understandable specialty.

Trenton’s team’s approach is to use sparse autoencoders to pull apart the features that are represented together in the activations. If you applied that to Mixtral, you could ask: Are the same features replicated across experts? Are some features concentrated in particular experts? What information is the router using to make its decisions?

That would help distinguish between experts having meaningful specializations and the architecture just being a convenient way to get more capacity for a given amount of compute. And you could test it causally—intervene on a feature or change the routing and see whether the model’s behavior changes in the way your interpretation predicts. It seems like a fairly concrete project where you could learn something about both interpretability and why mixture-of-experts models work.
